userStories.title: Global 402 interceptor — PaywallContext (BIL-007)
userStories.description:
Create a PaywallContext React context provider that wraps the app. Intercepts all API responses from apiFetch. When a 402 status is received: (1) Parse the response body for { requiredPlan, currentPlan, upgradeUrl }, (2) Store the blocked feature info in context state, (3) Trigger PaywallModal (US-041) to display. The context exposes: { isPaywalled, blockedFeature, requiredPlan, dismissPaywall, checkPlan }. checkPlan(feature) can be called proactively by UI components to disable buttons before the user clicks (e.g., disable 'Run Pipeline' button for free users). Wrap in src/App.tsx alongside other context providers.

## Context
- **apiFetch interceptor pattern**: Modify `src/lib/apiFetch` (or wrap it) to detect 402 status codes. Do NOT use a global `fetch` monkey-patch — keep interception scoped to Rorca's API client. The existing `apiFetch` likely throws or returns on non-2xx; add 402 as a special case before the generic error path.

- **Context provider ordering in App.tsx**: `PaywallContext` must be placed *inside* `AuthContext`/`WorkspaceContext` (needs user plan info) but *outside* route components so every panel can consume it. Check existing provider nesting in `src/App.tsx` — likely `AuthProvider > WorkspaceProvider > ThemeProvider > ...`. Insert PaywallProvider after Auth so `useAuth()` is available for `GET /api/users/me` re-fetch.

- **Plan gating data source**: `checkPlan(feature)` needs a feature→plan mapping. This should come from the backend (e.g., `GET /api/users/me` returning `{ plan, features: [...] }` or a static plan matrix). Do NOT hardcode plan gates in the frontend — they'll drift from backend 402 logic. If backend doesn't expose a plan matrix yet, `checkPlan` should optimistically allow and rely on 402 interception as the authoritative gate.

- **PaywallModal is a separate story (US-041 references itself)**: This story creates the *context and interception logic*. The modal component may be defined here as a minimal placeholder or imported if already built. Ensure the context sets state that a modal component can consume — don't couple modal rendering tightly into the context provider itself.

- **Error resilience on 402 body parsing**: Use `try/catch` around `response.json()` — a 402 from a reverse proxy or malformed backend response should fall through to a generic "Upgrade required" state, not crash the app. Use Zod `safeParse` with `z.object({ requiredPlan: z.string(), currentPlan: z.string(), upgradeUrl: z.string().url() })` for validation.

- **Zero overhead when not paywalled**: Use a simple boolean `isPaywalled` flag in context state. Don't re-render the entire tree on plan check — memoize context value with `useMemo` keyed on `isPaywalled`, `blockedFeature`, and `currentPlan`. `checkPlan()` should be a stable callback ref (`useCallback`) that reads from a ref or state without causing consumer re-renders.

- **Auth middleware is globally disabled** (per CLAUDE.md gotchas): The 402 interceptor may never fire in local dev since auth is bypassed. Add a dev-mode test hook or mock 402 response capability so the paywall flow can be verified without enabling auth. Consider a `?simulatePaywall=true` query param in dev mode only.

- **State reset after upgrade**: After `dismissPaywall()` following a successful upgrade, re-fetch `GET /api/users/me` and update plan state. Use the existing `AuthContext` or a dedicated user/plan fetch — don't duplicate the user endpoint call. Clear `blockedFeature` and `isPaywalled` only after confirming the new plan from the API response.

userStories.title: CSRF protection via double-submit cookie
userStories.description:
Implement CSRF protection using the double-submit cookie pattern across the entire backend. On login/session creation: generate a cryptographically random CSRF token (32 bytes, hex encoded), set it as a cookie (name: _csrf, SameSite=Strict, Secure in production, httpOnly=false so JS can read it). Frontend (apiFetch): read the _csrf cookie and include it in the X-CSRF-Token header on all state-changing requests (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE). Backend middleware: verify X-CSRF-Token header matches the _csrf cookie value on all state-changing requests. Skip CSRF check for: webhook endpoints (they use signature verification), health check. Return 403 Forbidden with { error: 'CSRF token mismatch' } on failure.

## Context

userStories.title: Structured error responses audit — replace raw error strings with AppError
userStories.description:
Audit all 32 backend route files for raw error response patterns and replace with AppError subclasses. Search patterns to find: `res.status(4xx).json({ error:`, `res.status(5xx).json({`, `throw new Error(`. Replace with: ValidationError (400), AuthError (401), ForbiddenError (403), NotFoundError (404), ConflictError (409), UnprocessableError (422). Ensure all error responses follow the shape { error: string, code?: string, details?: Record<string, unknown> }. The centralized error handler middleware in error-handler.ts catches AppError instances and serializes them. Target: zero raw res.status().json({ error: }) calls in route handlers.

## Context
- **AppError hierarchy is already defined** in `backend/src/lib/errors.ts` — import `ValidationError`, `AuthError`, `ForbiddenError`, `NotFoundError`, `ConflictError`, `UnprocessableError` from there. Do NOT create new error classes; use the existing ones with their immutable HTTP status codes.

- **Error handler middleware** lives in `backend/src/lib/error-handler.ts` (or similar) and already serializes `AppError` instances to `{ error, code, details }`. Verify it catches non-AppError `Error` instances and returns `500 { error: 'Internal server error' }` without stack trace leakage before starting route conversions — fix the middleware first if needed.

- **There are 32 route files** in `backend/src/routes/`. Use `grep -rn 'res\.status(4' backend/src/routes/` and `grep -rn 'res\.status(5' backend/src/routes/` and `grep -rn 'throw new Error(' backend/src/routes/` to get the full audit list before making changes. Work file-by-file to avoid partial conversions.

- **Pattern replacement rules**: `res.status(400).json({ error: msg })` → `throw new ValidationError(msg)`, `res.status(404)` → `throw new NotFoundError(msg)`, `res.status(409)` → `throw new ConflictError(msg)`, `res.status(401)` → `throw new AuthError(msg)`, `res.status(403)` → `throw new ForbiddenError(msg)`, `res.status(422)` → `throw new UnprocessableError(msg)`. For 500s, let unhandled errors propagate to the middleware rather than catching and re-throwing.

- **Gotcha: early-return patterns** — many routes use `if (!found) return res.status(404).json(...)` as a guard clause. When converting to `throw new NotFoundError(...)`, remove the `return` keyword since `throw` already exits the function. Also ensure the route handler is wrapped in `async` + the error handler catches async rejections (Express 5 does this natively; Express 4 needs `express-async-errors` or explicit try/catch or a wrapper).

- **Do not touch success responses** — only convert error paths (`res.status(4xx)` and `res.status(5xx)`). Leave `res.json(data)`, `res.status(200)`, and `res.status(201)` calls untouched. The acceptance criteria target is zero raw error responses, not zero `res.status()` calls overall.

- **Memory: always add tests for edge cases** — per project convention, add or update Jest tests that verify at least one route throws the correct AppError subclass and that the error handler serializes it properly. A single integration test hitting the error handler with each AppError subclass is sufficient.

- **Auth middleware is globally disabled** (intentional for local tool) — `AuthError` throws will still be caught by the error handler, but no routes currently enforce auth. Don't add auth checks as part of this audit; just ensure the error class mapping is correct for any existing 401 responses.

Database: ping query (SELECT 1), check pool stats. Worker: check worker_heartbeat table (stale if last_seen > 90s). GitHub: check last integration_health entry. ## Context
- **Route file**: Health endpoint is in `backend/src/routes/health.ts` — read existing implementation before modifying. The route is mounted without auth middleware (intentional for monitoring tools).
- **Database pool stats**: Access `pool.totalCount`, `pool.idleCount`, `pool.waitingCount` from the `pg` Pool instance exported by `backend/src/db/index.ts`. Latency: wrap `SELECT 1` in `Date.now()` delta. Do NOT use `pool.connect()` for the ping — use `pool.query()` to avoid checkout/release overhead.
- **Worker heartbeat**: Query `worker_heartbeat` table — column is `last_seen` (timestamptz). Stale threshold is 90s (`NOW() - last_seen > INTERVAL '90 seconds'`). Handle empty result (no rows = worker never started) as distinct from stale.
- **Migration status**: `schema_migrations` table tracks applied migrations (BIGINT `version` column). Compare against files in `backend/src/db/pg-migrations/` to compute pending count. Be aware of hybrid numbering: sequential (001–079) and timestamp format coexist.
- **Promise.allSettled**: Run all component checks in parallel to meet the 500ms SLA. Catch individual failures gracefully — a failing GitHub check must not bring down the entire health endpoint.
- **Error handling**: Return HTTP 503 (not 500) when database is unreachable. Use `res.status(503).json(...)` directly — do NOT throw `AppError` since the health endpoint must always return structured JSON even in failure states.
- **Package version**: Use `require('../../package.json').version` or read from a build-time constant. Do NOT use `fs.readFileSync` at request time — cache at module load.
- **AGE gotcha**: If the health check query runs on a pool connection that was previously poisoned by AGE `search_path`, `SELECT 1` still works but any table query might hit wrong schema. - **Script location & language**: `scripts/generate-changelog.ts` — use `tsx` to run (already in devDependencies). Keep it a standalone script with no additional npm dependencies; use Node.js built-in `child_process.execSync` for git commands and `fs` for file I/O.
- **Conventional commit parsing**: Split on first `:` after the prefix. Handle scoped prefixes like `feat(US-001):` and `fix(backend):`. Map: `feat:` → Added, `fix:` → Fixed, `refactor:` → Changed, `chore:`/`ci:`/`docs:`/`build:`/`test:` → ignore (skip from changelog). Anything without a recognized prefix → "Other" section (AC requirement — do not silently drop).
- **Git tag ordering**: Use `git tag --list 'v*' --sort=version:sort` for semver-correct ordering. For the range between tags, use `git log v0.1.0..v0.2.0 --pretty=format:"%s"`. For the first tag, use `git log v0.1.0 --pretty=format:"%s"` (all commits up to that tag).
- **GitHub compare URLs**: Construct as `https://github.com/getrorca/rorca/compare/v{prev}...v{current}`. For the first version, link to the tag itself: `https://github.com/getrorca/rorca/releases/tag/v0.1.0`. Do not hardcode the GitHub org/repo — extract from `git remote get-url origin` and parse, falling back to `getrorca/rorca`.
- **Empty state handling**: When `git tag --list 'v*'` returns nothing, generate a single `## [Unreleased]` section with all commits categorized. This satisfies the "Initial release" AC without inventing a fake version number.
- **Keep a Changelog format gotcha**: The spec says "Keep a Changelog format" — this requires a preamble header (`# Changelog\n\nAll notable changes...`) and an `[Unreleased]` section at the top for commits after the latest tag. Don't skip these structural elements.
- **Integration with US-013 release workflow**: The release workflow should call `npx tsx scripts/generate-changelog.ts` and then `git add CHANGELOG.md` before creating the GitHub Release. Keep the script idempotent — it overwrites `CHANGELOG.md` entirely on each run (no append/merge logic needed). The release workflow integration should be a single line addition, not a refactor.
- **Performance**: The 10-second budget for 1000 commits is generous. The bottleneck is `git log` calls per tag range — batch into a single `git log --all --pretty=format:"%H %s" --decorate=short` and parse tag boundaries in-memory rather than spawning N subprocesses (one per tag pair). This also avoids shell injection if tag names contain special characters — use `execFileSync` over `execSync` for safety.

userStories.title: Email/Password Auth Backend Hardening
userStories.description:
Harden POST /api/auth/register and POST /api/auth/login with input validation, bcrypt hashing at cost 12, rate limiting on failed attempts, and non-enumerable error responses to prevent user discovery attacks.

## Context
- **Auth routes exist at `backend/src/routes/auth.ts`** — read current register/login handlers before modifying. Auth middleware is globally disabled (intentional for local tool), so these routes handle their own validation. Don't re-enable global `authRequired`.
- **Use Zod validation middleware pattern** (`validateBody(schema)`) for email/password input validation, consistent with project conventions. Use `safeParse` not `.parse()`. Return `{ error, details }` shape via `ValidationError` (400) or `UnprocessableError` (422) from `backend/src/lib/errors.ts`.
- **Error responses must use AppError hierarchy** — `UnprocessableError` for 422, `ConflictError` for 409, `AuthError` for 401. HTTP 423 (Locked) is non-standard for AppError — you'll need to either add a `LockedError` subclass or use `res.status(423).json(...)` directly with `Retry-After` header.
- **Constant-time comparison gotcha**: Always run `bcrypt.compare()` even when the email doesn't exist in the DB — compare against a dummy hash to prevent timing-based user enumeration. This is explicit in AC but easy to miss in implementation.
- **Rate limiting for failed logins is separate from the global `rate-limiter.ts`** (which is keyed on `userId:method:path`). The per-email lockout (5 attempts / 15 min) needs its own tracking — either a `login_attempts` DB table or an in-memory map keyed by email. DB-backed is more robust across backend restarts; in-memory is simpler and acceptable for a local tool.
- **Database helpers are async** — always `await` calls to `query<T>()`, `queryOne<T>()`, `execute()`. Use `$1, $2, ...` numbered placeholders. If adding a `login_attempts` table, create a migration with timestamp format `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_login_attempts.sql`.
- **bcrypt cost 12 ~250ms on modern hardware** — the 500ms endpoint response AC is achievable without async tricks, but don't add any synchronous blocking around the hash call. Use `bcrypt.hash(password, 12)` (async version), not `bcrypt.hashSync()`.
- **Non-enumerable error responses**: Register's "email already exists" 409 is acceptable per AC, but login must return identical `401 "Invalid email or password"` for both unknown-email and wrong-password cases. Verify no error message leaks in catch blocks or validation middleware.

userStories.title: Password Reset Flow
userStories.description:
Implement a secure two-step password reset: POST /api/auth/forgot-password generates a cryptographic token and stores its hash with 1-hour expiry; POST /api/auth/reset-password validates the token, updates the password hash, and invalidates all existing refresh tokens for that user.

## Context
- **Migration**: Create `password_reset_tokens` table via a new timestamp-prefixed migration (`YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_password_reset_tokens.sql`). Columns: `id` (serial PK), `user_id` (FK → `users.id`), `token_hash` (text, indexed), `expires_at` (timestamptz), `used_at` (timestamptz nullable). Use `$1, $2, ...` numbered placeholders in all queries.

- **Route structure**: Add two new routes in `backend/src/routes/auth.ts` (or wherever existing auth routes live). Use Zod `validateBody()` middleware for both endpoints. `forgot-password` validates `{ email: z.string().email() }`; `reset-password` validates `{ token: z.string(), password: z.string().min(8) }` plus complexity regex. Always return 200 from forgot-password regardless of email lookup result — this is the anti-enumeration requirement.

- **Token generation**: Use `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')` for the raw token, store only `crypto.createHash('sha256').update(token).digest('hex')` in DB. On reset, hash the incoming token the same way and look up by hash. Never store or log the raw token.

- **Error handling**: Use the existing `AppError` hierarchy — `NotFoundError` for invalid/used tokens, `ValidationError` (422) for password complexity failures. For the 410 expired case, you'll need to either create a `GoneError` subclass or use `res.status(410).json({ error: '...' })` directly since there's no existing 410 class in `backend/src/lib/errors.ts`. Check what subclasses exist before deciding.

- **Refresh token invalidation**: On successful reset, `DELETE FROM refresh_tokens WHERE user_id = $1` to force re-auth on all devices. Wrap the password update + token mark-as-used + refresh token deletion in a `transaction()` call to ensure atomicity — if any step fails, none commit.

- **Password hashing**: Use the same bcrypt approach as the registration route (likely `bcrypt.hash(password, saltRounds)` — check `auth.ts` for the existing pattern and salt rounds). Do NOT introduce a different hashing library.

- **Gotcha — auth middleware is globally disabled**: Auth routes work but `authRequired` is commented out globally. Both new endpoints must be unauthenticated (forgot-password by design, reset-password uses token-based auth). Ensure neither endpoint accidentally depends on `req.user`.

- **Testing**: Add Jest tests covering: valid reset flow end-to-end, expired token (410), used token (404), non-existent token (404), weak password (422), anti-enumeration (200 for unknown email), refresh token cleanup after reset. Use `afterAll()` to clean up DB pool connections per testing conventions.

userStories.title: Frontend JWT Refresh Interceptor
userStories.description:
Create a fetch interceptor in src/lib/apiFetch.ts that transparently handles JWT expiry: on 401 response, attempt to refresh the access token using the stored refresh token, retry the original request, and redirect to /login on refresh failure. - `src/lib/apiFetch.ts` is the existing fetch wrapper — all API calls route through it. Modify this file directly; do not create a separate interceptor module.
- Auth middleware is globally disabled (`server.ts` line ~78, intentional for local single-user tool). The 401 interception logic will only activate if/when auth is re-enabled per-route. Ensure the interceptor is a no-op passthrough when no auth tokens exist rather than breaking unauthenticated flows.
- Auth routes are at `POST /api/auth/login`, `POST /api/auth/refresh`, `POST /api/auth/logout`. The refresh endpoint expects a refresh token (stored in `refresh_tokens` table). Exclude `/api/auth/login` and `/api/auth/refresh` from interception to prevent infinite loops.
- Use a module-scoped `let refreshPromise: Promise | null = null` pattern for request queuing — if a refresh is in-flight, subsequent 401 handlers await the same promise instead of firing new refresh calls. Reset to `null` on resolution.
- Toast notifications use `ToastContext` (`src/contexts/ToastContext.tsx`). Import and use `useToast()` or the standalone toast function if `apiFetch` is outside React tree — check how existing non-component code triggers toasts.
- Navigation to `/login` should use `window.location.href = '/login'` (not `react-router` navigate) since `apiFetch.ts` is a plain utility module outside the React component tree and has no access to router hooks.
- Token storage: check both `localStorage` and `cookies` for refresh token location — the codebase uses JWT with `refresh_tokens` DB table but client-side storage mechanism needs verification in existing auth code (`src/contexts/AuthContext.tsx`).
- Do NOT add error handling for scenarios that can't happen given the current auth-disabled state. Keep the interceptor minimal — it will be exercised when auth is re-enabled. Avoid over-engineering with retry limits, backoff, or complex state machines beyond the specified queue pattern.

userStories.title: Stripe Customer Portal Session Endpoint
userStories.description:
Implement POST /api/billing/create-portal-session that creates a Stripe Billing Portal session for the authenticated user and returns the session URL. Frontend navigates the user to the portal URL for self-service subscription management.

## Context
- **Route pattern**: Follow existing Express route conventions in `backend/src/routes/billing.ts`. Use `validateBody(schema)` middleware if accepting a request body, though this endpoint likely needs no body. Use `AppError` subclasses (`ValidationError` for missing subscription, custom 502/503 via `new AppError(msg, statusCode)`) — check how `errors.ts` handles non-standard status codes (502, 503 may need direct `res.status().json()` if `AppError` doesn't support them).

userStories.title: Trial Expiry Notification and Grace Period
userStories.description:
Implement automated trial expiry notifications: 3-day warning, expiry-day notice, 24-hour grace period with amber banner on pipeline runs, and automatic reversion to free plan after grace period.

## Context
- **pg-boss cron pattern**: Register the daily job using `boss.schedule('trial:expiry-check', '0 9 * * *', ...)` in `worker.ts`. Follow existing patterns from `pipeline:cron` job type — the worker already handles cron registration and polling. Add the new queue name to the job type documentation in `worker.ts`.

- **Users table schema**: The story assumes `users.plan` and `users.trial_ends_at` columns exist. Verify these exist in migrations 001–079; if not, create a new timestamp-prefixed migration (`YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_trial_fields.sql`) adding `plan VARCHAR DEFAULT 'free'` and `trial_ends_at TIMESTAMPTZ` to `users`. Use `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` for idempotency.

- **requirePlan middleware**: This is a new middleware — model it after the existing `authRequired` pattern but check `users.plan` instead of JWT validity. Return 402 (Payment Required) with `{ error: 'Plan upgrade required', code: 'PLAN_REQUIRED' }`. Note: auth middleware is globally disabled, so `requirePlan` must be mounted explicitly on pipeline trigger routes, not globally.

- **WAL event emission**: Use `INSERT INTO wal_events (event_type, payload, ts)` with `ts` column (NOT `created_at` — see gotcha in CLAUDE.md). Event types `plan_reverted` and `notification_dispatch_failed` are new additions to the WAL vocabulary. Emit WAL events via direct DB insert from the worker process (not via `fetch` to `/api/wal` — that's for execution-engine subprocesses; the worker has direct DB access).

- **Grace period field on runs endpoint**: `GET /api/pipeline/runs` must join against `users` to compute `graceExpiresAt` (= `trial_ends_at + INTERVAL '24 hours'`). Only include this field when the user's plan is in trial-expired state — don't pollute the response for paying users. The frontend amber banner should use a countdown timer (client-side interval), not polling.

- **Error tolerance / partial completion**: Process users in a loop with individual try/catch per user — do NOT wrap all notifications in a single transaction. This satisfies the "partial notifications are not rolled back" requirement. Log failures per-user and continue. The WAL `notification_dispatch_failed` event acts as the retry signal for the next cron run.

- **Notification creation**: Use the existing `notification_history` table and `notification-dispatcher.ts` patterns for in-app notifications. Check `notification_subscriptions` for user preferences, but trial expiry notifications should bypass channel preferences (always deliver in-app — these are system-critical).

- **Empty state optimization**: Query `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE trial_ends_at IS NOT NULL AND plan = 'pro_trial'` before iterating. If zero, log `'No active trials to process'` and return early — avoid unnecessary iteration or notification queries.
acceptanceCriteria: A pg-boss cron job runs daily at 09:00 UTC and creates an in-app notification for users whose trial expires in exactly 3 days: 'Your Pro trial expires in 3 days. Upgrade to keep pipeline execution.'

If no users have active trials (empty state), the daily cron job completes immediately with log message 'No active trials to process'
If the cron job fails mid-execution (error state), partial notifications that were already created are not rolled back — failed users are retried on next cron run

userStories.title: Plan Enforcement Guard for Active Pipeline Runs
userStories.description:
When a plan change is triggered (trial expiry, subscription cancellation, or downgrade), check for in-progress pipeline runs. If an active run exists, defer the plan change until the run completes. Apply immediately if no run is active.

## Context
- **DB schema**: Story requires adding `plan_transition_pending BOOLEAN DEFAULT false` and `pending_plan TEXT` columns to the `users` table. Use timestamp-format migration (`YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_plan_transition_pending.sql`). The `users` table already exists (see migrations 001+).

- **pg-boss cron job pattern**: Follow the existing `pipeline:cron` pattern in `worker.ts` for the hourly force-apply job. Register as a named schedule (e.g., `plan-transition-sweep`) with `boss.schedule()`. Worker must be running for this to fire — document this dependency. Use `boss.work('plan:force-apply', handler)` pattern consistent with existing queue handlers (`pipeline:run`, `pipeline:retry`, `pipeline:cancel`).

- **WAL event emission**: Use `emitWalEvent()` or direct INSERT into `wal_events` table. Column is `ts` (NOT `created_at`). Event type `plan_force_applied` with `payload` as JSONB `{ userId, staleSince }`. Follow existing WAL event patterns in `execution-engine.ts`.

- **Run completion hook**: The run status transition to `completed`/`failed`/`cancelled` happens in multiple places — `execution-engine.ts` (normal completion), `worker.ts` (cancel handler), and stale recovery (`recoverStaleJobs`). The plan transition check must fire in ALL completion paths, not just the happy path. Consider a shared `onRunCompleted(runId)` helper to avoid duplication.

- **Transaction safety**: The "apply immediately if no active run" path must use `transaction<T>(fn)` from `db/index.ts` to atomically check `pipeline_runs` status AND update `users.plan` — otherwise a race condition allows a run to start between the check and the update.

- **Middleware pattern**: `requirePlan` middleware should read `users.plan` (current), not `pending_plan`. This is explicitly called out in AC but easy to get wrong. The middleware likely lives alongside existing auth middleware patterns in `backend/src/lib/`.

- **Billing route**: `GET /api/billing/status` — check if this route already exists in `backend/src/routes/billing.ts`. If so, extend the response shape. Add `@swagger` JSDoc annotation for OpenAPI spec generation (API-first pattern). Response shape: `{ plan, planTransitionPending, pendingPlan }`.

- **Error handling**: On force-apply DB failure, do NOT throw — log the error and leave `plan_transition_pending=true` for next hourly sweep. Use `console.error` or structured logger, not `AppError` (this is a background job, not a request handler).
acceptanceCriteria: On plan change trigger, if a pipeline_runs row with status='running' exists for the workspace, set users.plan_transition_pending=true and users.pending_plan='free' without modifying users.plan

If no active pipeline run exists at plan change trigger time (empty state), apply plan change immediately within the same DB transaction — plan_transition_pending remains false

plan_transition_pending rows older than 24 hours are force-applied by a pg-boss cron job running every hour; force-apply creates WAL event with event_type 'plan_force_applied' and payload { userId, staleSince }
GET /api/billing/status returns { plan, planTransitionPending, pendingPlan } so frontend can show amber banner: 'Plan change pending — will apply after current run completes'
Force-apply does not interrupt an actively running pipeline run; it only applies if status is no longer 'running' at time of force-apply check (error prevention)
If the plan transition DB update fails (error state), the error is logged and plan_transition_pending remains true for retry on next check
While plan transition is pending (loading state), requirePlan middleware continues to enforce the current (not pending) plan until transition completes

userStories.title: OG image generation script for landing pages
userStories.description:
Create static OG images (1200x630px) for each landing page route: home, architecture, engine, compute, pricing, and download. Store as pre-generated PNGs in landing-page/public/og/. Each image uses the zinc-950 dark background with Rorca logo and page-specific title and tagline.

## Context
- **This is a landing page asset task, not a backend/API task.** All work happens in the `landing-page/` directory (Next.js 14 + Tailwind v4, port 3002). Do not touch anything in `backend/` or `src/`.
- **OG image generation approach:** Use `@vercel/og` (satori-based) or `sharp` with a Node.js build script (e.g., `landing-page/scripts/generate-og.ts`). Prefer `sharp` for static PNG generation since `@vercel/og` is optimized for runtime/edge — but either satisfies the AC. The script must be runnable via `npx tsx landing-page/scripts/generate-og.ts` and exit code 1 on failure.
- **zinc-950 background is `#09090b`** — this is the Tailwind zinc-950 value. Hardcode it in the generation script; do not pull from Tailwind config at build time (unnecessary complexity).
- **US-009 dependency:** The meta tags story (US-009) must already define `<meta property="og:image">` per route. This story wires the `og/{pagename}.png` path into those tags using `NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`. Verify US-009's meta tag component exists before modifying it — read the layout or head component first.
- **`NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` fallback:** In Next.js, `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is inlined at build time. The fallback to `http://localhost:3002` with `console.warn` must happen in the shared OG URL helper, not repeated per page. Keep it as a single utility function.
- **Commit PNGs to repo:** The AC explicitly requires static assets committed to git. Do not add `landing-page/public/og/*.png` to `.gitignore`. These are small files (1200x630 PNGs ~30-80KB each) — acceptable for version control.
- **Fallback logic for `og-default.png`:** The build-time warning ("Missing OG image for {page}") implies a validation step — either in the OG generation script itself or a separate check. The simplest approach: the generation script produces all 6 + default, then a post-generation validation loop checks each expected file exists.
- **No over-engineering:** Do not create a dynamic OG image API route (`/api/og`), do not add a CMS for taglines, do not integrate with the backend. This is a one-time static asset generation script with 7 output files.

userStories.title: GitHub OAuth Minimal Scope Strategy with Incremental Upgrade
userStories.description:
Change the initial GitHub OAuth flow to request only user:email and public_repo scopes. When a user attempts a feature requiring the repo scope (private repos), trigger an incremental OAuth upgrade flow with an explanation modal. Store granted scopes in github_connections.scopes.

## Context
- **Migration format**: New `scopes TEXT[]` column on `github_connections` must use timestamp-prefixed migration file (`YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_github_connections_scopes.sql`). Use `ALTER TABLE github_connections ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS scopes TEXT[]` inside a transaction. Clean up pool connections in any test `afterAll()`.

- **OAuth route location**: GitHub OAuth routes live in `backend/src/routes/` (check for existing `github.ts` or `webhooks.ts` route file). The authorization URL construction and callback handler both need modification. Inspect the existing OAuth flow before changing scopes — the redirect URI, state parameter, and token exchange logic must remain intact.

- **Error response pattern**: The 403 with `{ error, requiredScope, upgradeRequired }` should use the `AppError` hierarchy — likely a `ForbiddenError` subclass or a custom error shape. Existing pattern: throw from route handlers, `error-handler.ts` catches and serializes to `{ error, code, details }`. The `upgradeRequired: true` field is non-standard — add it via the `details` object or extend the error shape explicitly.

- **Scope check middleware**: Create a reusable middleware or helper (e.g., `requireGitHubScope('repo')`) that queries `github_connections.scopes` for the active workspace's GitHub connection. For `NULL` scopes (pre-migration rows), treat as `['user:email', 'public_repo']` per AC — use `COALESCE(scopes, ARRAY['user:email','public_repo'])` in the query.

- **Token replacement on upgrade**: When the user completes the incremental OAuth flow with `repo` scope, the callback must replace the existing `access_token` and update `scopes` via array concatenation (`scopes || ARRAY['repo']`). Ensure the old token is invalidated or overwritten — GitHub OAuth tokens are per-app, so a new authorization replaces the previous one. Use `$1, $2, ...` numbered placeholders, not `?`.

- **Frontend modal pattern**: Check existing modal/dialog patterns in `src/components/` — Rorca likely has a shared modal component (possibly via command palette or spec review slide-over). The upgrade modal needs three states: default (Authorize/Cancel buttons), loading (spinner + disabled buttons during redirect), and error. Toast on cancel should use the existing `ToastContext`.

- **AGE search_path gotcha**: If any GitHub connection queries touch Apache AGE graph operations, restore `search_path` after. Standard `query<T>()` helper from `db/index.ts` is safe; only direct `pool.connect()` + `setupAgeSession()` calls need cleanup.

- **Security**: Never log or expose the GitHub OAuth `client_secret` or `access_token` in error responses. Store tokens in the existing `github_connections` table (already encrypted or handled). The `state` parameter in OAuth must be validated on callback to prevent CSRF.

userStories.title: Billing Webhook Idempotency
userStories.description:
Create a processed_webhooks table to track handled Stripe events. Before processing any webhook event, check for duplicate event IDs and return 200 immediately if already processed. Use a transaction to atomically process the event and record it. Add a pg-boss cleanup cron job for records older than 30 days.

## Context
- **Migration format**: Use timestamp prefix `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_processed_webhooks.sql` for the new migration. Table goes in the `rorca` schema (default search_path). Use `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` for idempotent migration.
- **DB helpers**: Use `transaction<T>(fn)` from `backend/src/db/index.ts` to wrap event processing + INSERT atomically. Use `queryOne<T>()` for the duplicate check (returns `T|undefined` — truthy means already processed). Use `$1, $2, ...` numbered placeholders, never `?`.
- **Unique constraint race condition**: Catch PostgreSQL error code `23505` (unique_violation) on the INSERT. Do NOT use a generic catch — only swallow this specific error and return 200. All other errors should propagate as 500.
- **pg-boss cron job**: Register as `webhook:cleanup` queue in `worker.ts` using `boss.schedule()` with cron expression `0 2 * * *`. Follow the existing pattern from `pipeline:cron` registration. Log deleted row count via `execute()` which returns `{ rowCount }`.
- **WAL event on cron failure**: Use `INSERT INTO wal_events` with `event_type = 'cron_cleanup_failed'` and timestamp column `ts` (NOT `created_at` — the `wal_events` table uses `ts`).
- **Webhook route placement**: Add to existing `backend/src/routes/webhooks.ts`. Use `@swagger` JSDoc annotation for OpenAPI auto-generation. No auth middleware needed (Stripe signature verification replaces auth). Verify Stripe signature via `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent()` before any DB operations.
- **Error handling**: Return `res.json({ status: 'already_processed' })` with 200 for duplicates — do NOT use AppError hierarchy for this (it's a success case). Only throw/return 500 for actual DB transaction failures.
- **Performance**: The duplicate check SELECT should be fast on `stripe_event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY` (implicit B-tree index). No additional index needed. The 50ms SLA for duplicate detection is easily met with a single PK lookup.

userStories.title: Self-Hosted Offline License Activation
userStories.description:
After Stripe checkout success, display the signed license JWT as a copyable key. Add a license activation input in Settings > Billing that verifies the RSA signature offline using the embedded public key and stores the license in ~/.rorca/license.json.

## Context
- **RSA key management**: Embed the RS256 public key as a constant in the backend (e.g., `backend/src/lib/license.ts`), never load it from an external URL. Use Node.js built-in `crypto.verify` or `jsonwebtoken` library with `algorithms: ['RS256']` — do NOT allow algorithm switching (prevents `alg: none` attacks). The private key for signing must live server-side only (Stripe webhook handler), never shipped to client.

- **File permissions on macOS/Linux**: `fs.writeFileSync` with `mode: 0o600` for `license.json`, `fs.mkdirSync` with `mode: 0o700` for `~/.rorca/`. Use `os.homedir()` to resolve `~` — do not shell out. On Windows (if ever supported), these permission flags are no-ops; document this limitation.

- **JWT verification is synchronous** — `jsonwebtoken.verify()` is CPU-bound but fast (<1ms for RS256). The "loading state" and 2-second spinner UX is for perceived reliability, not actual latency. Still wrap in async handler for consistency with the codebase's async-first pattern.

- **Stripe webhook handler**: The `billing` table already exists (see migrations). Add `license_key TEXT` column via a new timestamp-prefixed migration (`YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_billing_license_key.sql`). Webhook must verify Stripe signature (`stripe.webhooks.constructEvent`) before generating the JWT — this is the security boundary.

- **Validation pattern**: Use `validateBody(z.object({ licenseKey: z.string().min(1) }))` middleware on the activation endpoint. Error responses must use `UnprocessableError` (422) from `backend/src/lib/errors.ts` — do not return raw strings. Date formatting for expiry message: use `new Date(exp * 1000).toISOString().split('T')[0]` for `YYYY-MM-DD`.

- **Frontend clipboard**: Use `navigator.clipboard.writeText()` with a fallback for older browsers. The "Copied!" tooltip with 2-second revert is a common pattern in the codebase — check existing copy-to-clipboard implementations (e.g., in `SpecDetailSlideOver` or similar) for consistency.

- **Auth is globally disabled** (intentional per CLAUDE.md), so the activation endpoint won't have `req.user` from `authRequired` middleware. If user identification is needed for storing the license in the `billing` table, the endpoint must accept a user identifier in the request or derive it from the license JWT claims themselves.

- **No outbound network calls**: The acceptance criteria explicitly requires offline verification. Do NOT call Stripe API, JWKS endpoints, or any external service during `POST /api/billing/activate-license`. All verification must use the locally embedded public key. This is the core design constraint — test it by mocking/blocking network in Jest tests.

userStories.title: Account Deletion and GDPR Right-to-Erasure
userStories.description:
Implement DELETE /api/users/me requiring password confirmation. Hard-delete personal data, anonymize operational records, and preserve workspace/spec data per privacy policy. Frontend shows 'Delete Account' button with confirmation modal in Settings > Account.

## Context
- **Auth middleware is globally disabled** but this story explicitly requires password confirmation via bcrypt — implement auth check inline within the `DELETE /api/users/me` handler (compare `req.body.password` against the user's stored hash). Since there's no global `authRequired`, you'll need to identify the user from the JWT/session manually or use a route-level `authRequired` middleware on just this endpoint.

- **Transaction ordering is critical**: The hard-delete cascade must respect FK constraints. Delete child tables first (refresh_tokens, vault_keys, github_connections, notification_subscriptions, notification_history, billing, password_reset_tokens, processed_webhooks) then the parent `users` row last. Use `transaction<T>(fn)` from `db/index.ts` to wrap the entire operation. The anonymization UPDATEs (`pipeline_runs.triggered_by`, `story_comments.author_id`) must happen BEFORE the `users` DELETE to avoid FK violations.

- **Use `$1, $2, ...` numbered placeholders** (not `?`) for all PostgreSQL queries. Use `execute()` helper for DELETE/UPDATE statements (returns `{ rowCount }`). Empty `rowCount: 0` is a valid success case per AC — do not throw on zero affected rows.

- **Error handling**: Throw `ValidationError` for missing password field (400), `AuthError` for incorrect password (401), `ConflictError` for active pipeline runs (409). These are caught by the centralized `errorHandler` middleware and serialized to `{ error, code, details }`.

- **Active run check query**: `SELECT id FROM pipeline_runs WHERE status = 'running' AND workspace_id IN (SELECT id FROM workspaces WHERE owner_id = $1) LIMIT 1`. Be aware that stale runs (process died but status still 'running') could permanently block deletion — consider whether to document this edge case or handle it.

- **Frontend modal**: Use existing `ToastContext` for the success toast. After successful `DELETE`, clear tokens from localStorage/sessionStorage, show toast, then `setTimeout(() => navigate('/'), 3000)`. Disable all interactive elements during the loading state per AC.

- **Migration**: If `pipeline_runs.triggered_by` or `story_comments.author_id` don't already support the needed values/nullability, add a timestamp-prefixed migration (e.g., `20260315000000_account_deletion_support.sql`). Check existing column types before creating unnecessary migrations.

- **Zod validation**: Use `validateBody(z.object({ password: z.string().min(1) }))` middleware on the route to get the 400 error for missing password field, consistent with project validation patterns.
acceptanceCriteria: DELETE /api/users/me requires request body { password: string }; returns 400 with error 'Password confirmation required' if field missing; returns 401 with error 'Incorrect password' if bcrypt comparison fails (error state)

If a pipeline_runs row with status='running' exists for any workspace owned by the user, returns 409 with error 'Cannot delete account while a pipeline run is active. Cancel all running pipelines first.' (error state)

On successful deletion, the following rows are hard-deleted in order within a single transaction: refresh_tokens, vault_keys, github_connections, notification_subscriptions, notification_history, billing, password_reset_tokens, processed_webhooks, users

pipeline_runs.triggered_by is set to 'deleted_user' (string literal) and story_comments.author_id is set to NULL for all rows referencing the deleted userId — these updates occur in the same deletion transaction

Settings > Account 'Delete Account' button opens a modal with red header 'Delete Account', body text 'This action cannot be undone. Enter your password to confirm.', password input field, and 'Delete My Account' red button plus 'Cancel' button
After successful deletion, frontend clears all stored tokens, shows toast 'Your account has been deleted', and navigates to the landing page root URL after 3 seconds

If the user has no data in any of the cascade tables (empty state — fresh account with no runs, no vault keys, no connections), the transaction still succeeds without error — DELETE queries return rowCount 0 gracefully

While the deletion transaction is processing (loading state), modal shows 'Deleting your account...' with spinner, both buttons are disabled, and the password input is read-only to prevent re-submission

Create landing-page/src/app/changelog/page.tsx that reads CHANGELOG.md from the repository root at build time and renders it as a date-grouped page. Footer 'Product' column includes a Changelog link.

## Context
- This is a **Next.js 14 landing page** (`landing-page/src/app/changelog/page.tsx`) — use App Router conventions (`generateStaticParams`, `generateMetadata`, server components). - Read `CHANGELOG.md` from repo root using `fs.readFileSync` in a server component (not a client component). Use `path.resolve(process.cwd(), '../../CHANGELOG.md')` or equivalent relative path from `landing-page/` to repo root — verify the correct relative path by checking the directory structure.
- Parse H2 headers with regex matching `## [x.y.z] - YYYY-MM-DD` format (Keep Changelog convention). Use a robust parser — split on H2 boundaries, then parse H3 subheadings (Added/Changed/Fixed/Removed) within each section. Malformed headers that don't match the pattern should fall through to plain text rendering with `console.warn`.
- Reuse the existing landing page header/footer components — check `landing-page/src/app/layout.tsx` or `landing-page/src/components/` for the shared `<Header>` and `<Footer>` already used by other pages. Add the "Changelog" link to the Footer's Product column in the shared footer component.

- **Empty state**: wrap the `readFileSync` in a try/catch — if file missing or empty, return empty array from the data layer and render the "No changelog entries yet." message. Do NOT let the build fail.
- **Loading skeleton**: Create a `loading.tsx` file in the same route directory (Next.js App Router convention) with 3 pulsing skeleton cards using Tailwind `animate-pulse` classes matching the version card layout dimensions.

userStories.title: macOS Binary Notarization Documentation and Gatekeeper Workaround
userStories.description:
Add macOS Gatekeeper workaround documentation to docs/troubleshooting.md. Show macOS-specific install instructions on the /download page. Add a TODO comment in the GitHub Actions release workflow for future Apple Developer Program enrollment.

## Context
- **This story is documentation + conditional UI only** — no backend changes, no migrations, no API routes. Keep scope tight: one markdown file (`docs/troubleshooting.md`), one frontend component change (`/download` page), one YAML comment in the GitHub Actions workflow.

- **OS detection must be client-side only** — use `useEffect` + `useState` pattern to avoid SSR hydration mismatch. Initialize `showMacWarning = false`, set to `true` in `useEffect` after checking `navigator.userAgent` for `/mac/i`. This matches the project's React 18 hydration-safe patterns already used in other conditional UI (e.g., lazy-loaded panels with `Suspense`).

- **Amber info box styling** — use Tailwind utility classes consistent with existing warning/info patterns in the codebase (likely `bg-amber-50 border-amber-200 text-amber-800` or similar). Do not introduce new CSS files or styled-components. Check existing toast/notification styling in `src/contexts/ToastContext` for amber color tokens already in use.

- **Anchor link to troubleshooting** — the `Learn more` link should point to the relative path of `docs/troubleshooting.md#macos-gatekeeper`. Verify the exact route where docs are served (static file vs. rendered markdown) to construct the correct href.

- **GitHub Actions YAML comment** — locate the existing release workflow file (likely `.github/workflows/release.yml` or similar). Add the `# TODO` comment block directly on the macOS build step. Do not modify any actual build logic — comment only.

- **`xattr` error state documentation** — the troubleshooting section must cover the "No such xattr" non-error explicitly. Users who installed via `curl | sh` (pipe install script) won't have the quarantine flag, so the `xattr -d` command will fail harmlessly. Document this as expected behavior, not an error.

- **Empty state / fallback behavior** — if `navigator.userAgent` is empty string or undefined (rare but possible in headless browsers, Playwright tests, or SSR), default to hiding the macOS box. Never show platform-specific warnings as a fallback for all platforms. This also prevents the box from appearing during E2E test runs with Playwright.

- **No over-engineering** — do not add a generic OS detection utility, feature flag, or configuration option. A simple inline `useEffect` with a `navigator.userAgent` check is sufficient for this single use case.
acceptanceCriteria: docs/troubleshooting.md contains a section '## macOS Gatekeeper' with the exact command xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./rorca and an explanation of when to use it (after downloading from browser, not via curl install script)

/download page detects visitor OS as macOS via navigator.userAgent and conditionally renders an amber Info box with text 'macOS users: After downloading, you may need to allow Rorca in System Settings > Privacy & Security.' — box is not shown on non-macOS user agents
Amber info box on /download contains a 'Learn more' link to the #macos-gatekeeper anchor in the troubleshooting guide

GitHub Actions release workflow YAML file contains a comment block on the macOS build step: '# TODO: Add Apple Developer Program enrollment for proper notarization' with link to Apple notarization docs
docs/troubleshooting.md section also documents the alternative: right-click the binary in Finder and select 'Open' to bypass Gatekeeper on first launch without running xattr
If visitor OS detection is unavailable (SSR or navigator.userAgent is empty), the macOS info box is hidden by default — not shown as fallback on all platforms (empty state)
If the xattr command fails with 'No such xattr: com.apple.quarantine' (error state), troubleshooting doc explains this means the quarantine flag was never set and no action is needed

The /download page amber info box renders after client-side hydration only (not during SSR) via a useEffect that sets a showMacWarning state — prevents hydration mismatch between server and client (loading state)
